extracted.intended_audience: consumers and home-theater/gaming enthusiasts shopping for AV receivers
extracted.subtask_description: A consumer-facing buying guide and product-roundup for selecting the best AV receiver (2026), describing what features matter, how CNET tests receivers, and recommending models for different use cases (movies, music, gaming, power users).

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels (number / Dolby Atmos minimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Channels: If you’re looking for a Dolby Atmos receiver, the minimum number of channels is seven -- which is written as either 7.1 or 5.1.2 channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with as little as a pair of stereo speakers and add rear speakers and a subwoofer later. The number of powered channels determines how many speakers you can drive without external amplification; more channels are necessary for Atmos/height configurations and dedicated home theater rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (watts per channel / realism of specs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power specs are mostly made up, but anything over 100 watts per channel in stereo is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use published 'power in stereo' as a rough guide; higher per-channel wattage generally helps headroom for dynamics, but be skeptical of marketing numbers. Compare real-world listening performance and head-to-head tests rather than relying solely on nominal wattage.

rubrics_metrics.name: HDMI connectivity (number of inputs/outputs and versions)
rubrics_metrics.description: All modern components use the universal HDMI standard and so you should choose a receiver that has as many of these inputs as possible. If you want to connect two different displays -- a TV and a projector, for example -- all but the Yamaha offer a second HDMI output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rear-mounted HDMI inputs are more important than front-mounted (front ports are seldom hot-plugged). Look for HDMI version 2.1 for 4K/120Hz support and 8K compatibility; note which HDMI inputs are 8K-capable on the receiver. Keep extra HDMI cables on hand. If the TV has ARC/eARC, connect the receiver's HDMI ARC output to use TV audio and pass video easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video standards and format support (4K/120Hz, 8K, HDR formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bare minimum right now is support for HDR and Dolby Vision, and at least HDMI version 2.0 or better. Many models support 4K, HDR and 8K as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you own an Xbox Series X or want future-proofing, look for 4K/120Hz support. Be aware of historical firmware/compatibility bugs (e.g., early 8K/4K/120Hz issues); check manufacturer firmware updates and dealer notes. 8K content is currently rare, so prioritize solid 4K/120Hz and HDR handling unless you need 8K specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dolby Atmos and object-based audio capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most receivers over $500 include Dolby Atmos capability, but you don’t need to buy height speakers straight away. You can always add them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support are common at mid and higher price points. The perceptible benefit varies by content; mounting surrounds higher on a wall can approximate height effects without ceiling speakers. Evaluate real Atmos performance in movie test scenes rather than assuming identical results across models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wi‑Fi music streaming and supported streaming protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside Bluetooth, many models have onboard Wi-Fi connectivity for wireless music streaming. Standards to look for include Spotify Connect, Apple AirPlay and Google Cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multiroom setups or diverse streaming needs, prefer receivers that support multiple protocols (AirPlay 2, Spotify Connect, Google Cast). Manufacturer ecosystems (HEOS, MusicCast, Sonos compatibility, DTS Play-Fi) affect integration with other devices. The quality and convenience of the 'streaming suite' can be a major differentiator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streaming suite quality and integrations (voice assistants, multiroom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Streaming options include Google Cast, DTS Play‑Fi, Spotify Connect, Sonos, AirPlay and Bluetooth. Being able to request songs directly from Google Assistant or Amazon Alexa is a real boon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how complete the streaming suite is (ability to request songs, platform parity with competitors). For buyers using voice assistants or wanting multiroom, check native integrations (Google Assistant, Alexa) and proprietary multiroom systems (HEOS, MusicCast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analog and specialty inputs (phono input / turntable support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vinyl is still in the middle of a revival, and the NR6100 enables users to take advantage thanks to a dedicated phono input for turntables and record players that lack an onboard phono preamp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use a turntable, a built-in phono preamp or dedicated phono input is valuable. Check number and type of analog inputs; lack of a phono input can be a con for vinyl users. Consider two-way Bluetooth or headphone outputs if those use-cases matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and setup (room correction / ease of use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The TX‑RZ50 includes audiophile-level calibration called Dirac Live; the Sony offers Digital Cinema Auto Calibration IX with improved microphone and multiple seating positions. Dirac Live setup can be difficult; follow manufacturer instructions (use the supplied mic and apps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate calibration algorithm quality and setup complexity. Advanced room correction (Dirac Live, similar systems) can substantially improve performance but may require more complex setup. Some receivers offer powerful manual calibration options (speaker height/screen height adjustments) for enthusiasts who prefer manual tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound quality for movies vs music (versatility)
rubrics_metrics.description: I want to see how well a system performs with music and movies, as most people will want to do both. Systems that can perform well with both types of entertainment inevitably score the highest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some models skew cinematic (big, booming sound) while others are more musical and dynamic. Test with 4K Blu-ray/movie scenes for Atmos and dialog clarity, and use test music tracks for musicality. Prefer balanced performers unless you have a use-case-specific preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability, design and build quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onkyo offers easy setup, excellent usability, solid looks and useful features. The Yamaha offers excellent build quality. Poorly designed remote control is listed as a con for some models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess front-panel layout, on-screen setup/UI, remote ergonomics, chassis build quality, and the intuitiveness of mobile apps. Good usability reduces setup friction; physical build quality affects longevity and perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectivity breadth (number/types of inputs & outputs beyond HDMI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivers include analog inputs, multiple HDMI inputs/outputs, digital inputs, and occasionally legacy connections. Many receivers no longer offer composite/component legacy switching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the receiver supports the legacy devices you own (composite/component) and whether it offers enough rear inputs for all your sources. If you have an older TV lacking ARC, you may need both HDMI and optical cables; very old TVs may require high-end receivers that still provide legacy switching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaming-specific features (4K/120Hz, low latency, HDMI 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re a gamer, choose one which has HDMI 2.1 so it can transmit 4K/120Hz to a TV as well. The Sony STR‑AN1000 supports HDMI 2.1 (4K/120Hz), 8K outputs, and video standards like Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gamers should prioritize HDMI 2.1, 4K/120Hz passthrough, variable refresh rate handling, and low-latency handling. If a receiver lacks these, you can connect a console directly to the TV and use eARC for audio as a workaround.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value / price-to-performance and model positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When spending under $1,000, there are several similar-performing receivers; the short answer is whichever is available for the lowest price. The Onkyo TX‑NR6100 offers the best mix of usability and performance for the money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare price, features and real-world performance rather than specs alone. Consider whether step-up models (higher price) justify their cost via more power, more inputs, better calibration or additional features. Availability and street price often determine the best buy among similar models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer firmware/compatibility history and updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that all 2020 8K-compatible receivers were prone to a bug preventing them from displaying variable refresh rate video; Denon, Marantz and Yamaha announced fixes for existing models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether manufacturers have issued firmware fixes for known issues (4K/120Hz, VRR). Verify current compatibility with your consoles/TVs and consult dealer/manufacturer resources for updates before purchasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the reviewer tests (CNET Audio Lab methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: At CNET, I test audio equipment side-by-side against reference devices at a similar price. For receivers I watch test scenes from 4K Blu-ray or streaming and evaluate Dolby Atmos surround sound performance and dialog clarity. I also use several test music tracks and test streaming features such as Bluetooth and Wi‑Fi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging models, CNET uses head-to-head listening/viewing with reference gear, evaluates both movie and music performance, checks streaming and connectivity features, and rates devices on a 1–10 CNET Score that weighs pricing, quality, features and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiroom/ecosystem considerations (proprietary systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denon ups the ante to AirPlay 2 and the proprietary HEOS system. Yamaha has its own MusicCast system. Onkyo and Sony support multiple streaming standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you already have other products in a brand’s ecosystem, prefer a receiver that integrates with that ecosystem (HEOS, MusicCast, Sonos, etc.). Proprietary systems affect multiroom streaming and device parity across your home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical outputs for connecting displays (ARC/eARC and second HDMI output)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a relatively new TV you should be able to use a single cable — an HDMI cable — to connect your receiver to your television. If you want to connect two different displays -- a TV and a projector, for example -- look for a second HDMI output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the receiver has HDMI ARC/eARC support to send TV audio back to the receiver; if you use two displays, verify the availability of a second HDMI output. For TVs without ARC, you may need optical/extra cables.
